Source. The first four attacker-controlled bytes `00 00 00 20` are read as `size == 32`, and the parser records that the size word already accounts for 4 bytes of box header.
The next four input bytes are `64 69 53 54` (`diST`), so this root box is identified as `GF_ISOM_BOX_TYPE_DIST` and later dispatched to `diST_box_read()`.
Charging the type word increases `hdr_size` from 4 to 8 on this witness, making the full root-box header length explicit before payload-size arithmetic.
Using `size == 32` from step 1 and `hdr_size == 8` from step 3, the parser stores `newBox->size == 24`, the remaining payload length later seen as `s->size` in `diST_box_read()`.
Destination extent. Once the `diST` reader runs, it stages the incoming string in fixed stack buffer `str[1024]` instead of allocating from the 24-byte payload length carried in `s->size`.
The write index starts at 0 for the first byte copied into `str`.

Root cause. Loop continuation is controlled only by the later `if (!str[i]) break`; there is no `i < sizeof(str)` bound and no per-byte check of `s->size` before reading. The only box-size guard, `ISOM_DECREASE_SIZE(p, i)`, appears after the loop, so it cannot stop the out-of-bounds iteration.

All 1024 bytes at file offsets 8..1031 are nonzero (`20 ff ff ff ff ff` followed by 1018 spaces). The first 24 iterations consume the declared payload, but because step 7 never consults `s->size`, the loop continues through the extra file bytes. Across these 1024 executions the break never fires, `str[0..1023]` become attacker-controlled nonzero bytes, and `i` advances to 1024.
